newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. Dec consumer prices seen moderate.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. Dec consumer prices seen moderate.

text.p: The December U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) without its volatile food and energy prices is likely to be quite subdued, doing little to alter prospects for a Federal Reserve interest-rate hike, economists said.

However, after December's strong employment report pushed bond yields up sharply on Friday, the CPI, set for relesae on Tuesday, will be closely analyzed for signs of price pressures that might convince the Fed to nudge rates higher, they said.
Economists polled by Reuters predicted, on average, that the CPI rose 0.3 percent in December.
Without food and energy items, the so-called core CPI jumped 0.2 percent in December, the economists told Reuters.

"We think businessmen and retailers probably had to offer a lot of sale prices toward the close of the Christmas season," said Elliott Platt, managing director, economic research at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "We think that's the basic driving factor behind a continuation of reduced price pressures."
Platt said he looks for 0.2 percent gains in both the total and core CPI indices.

"The CPI should be like the PPI (Producer Price Index), a little worse on the headline number than you might have hoped for but good on the core," said Neal Soss, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
The December PPI, reported on Thursday, was up 0.5 percent overall, but up a slight 0.1 percent when food and energy items were deleted.

"Food is a pretty good size chunk of the CPI and it's coming down and energy is the bad boy this month," said Soss, who expects a 0.4 percent gain in the total CPI but only a 0.1 percent rise in the core inflation measure.
The implication for monetary policy of such a reading, Soss believes, is that the Fed will remain on hold.
"The Fed's on hold anyway," he said. "Of course, they're watching the labor market and they're watching inflation but that's their job. They're on hold."
William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds, expects a gain of 0.4 percent of 0.5 percent in the aggregate CPI.
"We're still processing higher energy costs," he said. "We saw that in the PPI."
Sullivan expects the December core CPI to be up a fairly firm 0.3 percent.
"That will be somewhat negative for the bond market," he said.
David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. said data that show the pace of the economy is quickening has made inflation data all the more important.
If the Fed tightens interest rates in the first half of the year, it will be a cautious move based on persuasive evidence of increasing inflation, Jones said.
"That's why we'll see more of a focus on price numbers," he said.
